These include Western chimpanzees, Pan troglodytes verus, (Boesch and Boesch, 1990; Sugiyama and Koman, 1979), bearded capuchin monkeys, Sapajus libidinosus, (Fragaszy et al., 2004; Ottoni and Izar, 2008; Falótico and Ottoni, 2016; Luncz et al., 2016a), long-tailed macaques Macaca fascicularis, (Malaivijitnond et al., 2007; Gumert et al., 2009; Luncz et al., 2017a)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claims.claim: Percussive stone tool use is practiced by one group of white faced capuchin monkeys (Cebus capucinus imitator).
claims.source: Although rare, percussive stone tool use is also practiced by a few species of non-human primates. These include Western chimpanzees, Pan troglodytes verus, (Boesch and Boesch, 1990; Sugiyama and Koman, 1979), bearded capuchin monkeys, Sapajus libidinosus, (Fragaszy et al., 2004; Ottoni and Izar, 2008; Falótico and Ottoni, 2016; Luncz et al., 2016a), long-tailed macaques Macaca fascicularis, (Malaivijitnond et al., 2007; Gumert et al., 2009; Luncz et al., 2017a) and one group of white faced capuchin monkeys, Cebus capucinus imitator (Barrett et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: Non-human primates create long lasting archaeological signatures comprised of lithic assemblages.
claims.source: These non-human primates, similarly to hominins, create long lasting archaeological signatures comprised of lithic assemblages (Mercader et al., 2002; Mercader et al., 2007; Proffitt et al., 2018; Falótico et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published archaeological studies.

claims.claim: Long-tailed macaques are the only Old-World monkeys who use stone tools in their daily foraging.
claims.source: Long-tailed macaques are the only Old-World monkeys who use stone tools in their daily foraging.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of fact about the uniqueness of long-tailed macaques among Old World monkeys.

claims.claim: Long-tailed macaques use tools primarily to prey on shellfish, including oysters, marine gastropods, crabs and mussels.
claims.source: This behaviour is mainly observed in populations that live along the ocean shores of Southern Thailand and Myanmar where long-tailed macaques use tools primarily to prey on shellfish, including oysters, marine gastropods, crabs and mussels (Gumert et al., 2009)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: Long-tailed macaques use tools to process sea almonds.
claims.source: This behaviour is mainly observed in populations that live along the ocean shores of Southern Thailand and Myanmar where long-tailed macaques use tools primarily to prey on shellfish, including oysters, marine gastropods, crabs and mussels (Gumert et al., 2009), as well as sea almonds (Falótico et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: Long-tailed macaques use tools to process oil palm nuts.
claims.source: This behaviour is mainly observed in populations that live along the ocean shores of Southern Thailand and Myanmar where long-tailed macaques use tools primarily to prey on shellfish, including oysters, marine gastropods, crabs and mussels (Gumert et al., 2009), as well as sea almonds (Falótico et al., 2017) and oil palm nuts (Luncz et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: Long-tailed macaques, like humans, use stone tools to kill prey and access meat.
claims.source: Long-tailed macaques, like humans, use stone tools to kill prey and access meat.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative statement about the function of stone tool use.

claims.claim: Percussive damage on distal pointed ends of the hammerstone has generally been associated with processing rock oysters.
claims.source: For example, percussive damage on distal pointed ends of the hammerstone has generally been associated with processing rock oysters (Tan et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research on use wear analysis.

claims.claim: Central pitting on a flat hammerstone face is associated with marine snail predation.
claims.source: whilst central pitting on a flat hammerstone face is associated with marine snail predation (Gumert et al., 2009; Haslam et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on use wear analysis.

claims.claim: Two long-tailed macaque populations on neighbouring islands (Koram and Nom Sao Island) used stone tools to process the same species of shellfish but selected different sized stone tools.
claims.source: The results from this study showed that both macaque groups used stone tools to process the same species of shellfish, however the two groups selected different sized stone tools (Luncz et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work by the authors.

claims.claim: Differences in tool selection between Koram and Nom Sao Island macaques were related to varying prey sizes on each island.
claims.source: After comparing underlying ecological factors, potentially affecting this disparity in tool size selection, our data suggested that the differences in tool selection were related to the varying prey sizes on each island.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from data analysis in prior published work.

claims.claim: Differences in prey size between Koram and Nom Sao Island were associated with overharvesting and resource depletion through increased predation pressure.
claims.source: Differences in prey size were associated with overharvesting and resource depletion through increased predation pressure on one island.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from ecological data in prior published work.

claims.claim: Macaques preferentially target larger prey, leading to a reduction in the available prey populations and resulting in an overabundance of smaller, sexually immature prey specimens on the more heavily populated Koram Island.
claims.source: Maximising foraging efforts, macaques appear to preferentially target larger prey, leading to a reduction in the available prey populations and resulting in an overabundance of smaller, sexually immature prey specimens on the more heavily populated Koram Island, in turn leading to the use of smaller hammerstones.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from behavioral and ecological observations in prior published work.

claims.claim: On Nom Sao Island, the prey population remained abundant and significantly larger in size, resulting in the use of larger hammerstones.
claims.source: Conversely, on the less populated neighbouring island of Nom Sao, the prey population remained abundant and significantly larger in size, resulting in the use of larger hammerstones.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from ecological and archaeological data in prior published work.

claims.claim: The earliest repeated shellfish exploitation is known to have occurred in South Africa during the Middle Stone Age (MSA) and Later Stone Age (LSA).
claims.source: The earliest repeated shellfish exploitation is known to have occurred in South Africa during the Middle Stone Age (MSA) and Later Stone Age (LSA) (Steele and Klein, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published archaeological research.

claims.claim: Chronological variations in shellfish sizes found in archaeological middens from both MSA and LSA have been used as proxies for hominin population increases.
claims.source: Chronological variations in shellfish sizes found in archaeological middens from the both MSA and LSA have been used as proxies for hominin population increases.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about archaeological methodology supported by the context of cited literature.

claims.claim: Increased shellfish collection during the LSA compared to the MSA has been used to argue for and against a long and short chronology for the appearance of modern human behaviour.
claims.source: Increased shellfish collection during the LSA compared to the MSA (Sealy and Galimberti, 2011) has been used to argue for and against a long and short chronology for the appearance of modern human behaviour (Mcbrearty and Brooks, 2000; Klein, 2008; Steele and Klein, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published archaeological debates.

claims.claim: Changing environmental factors may have been a contributing factor in shellfish size variation in archaeological middens.
claims.source: However, others have also suggested that changing environmental factors may have been a contributing factor in this shellfish size variation (Sealy and Galimberti, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research proposing alternative explanations.

claims.claim: Two island dwelling populations of long-tailed macaques in the Ao Phang Nga National Park, at Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay (~9 km apart), routinely use stone tools to process the same marine resources.
claims.source: During exploratory pilot fieldwork on the western side of peninsular Thailand in the Andaman Sea, approximately 500 km southeast of the previous study site in Khao Sam Roi Yot National Park, we identified two island dwelling populations in the Ao Phang Nga National Park, at Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay (~9 km apart; Figure 1) who routinely use stone tools to process the same marine resources.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on direct field observations by the researchers and is illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: A total of 115 stone tools were analysed from both Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay locations combined.
claims.source: In total, we analysed 115 stone tools combined from both locations (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the sample size analyzed in the study, with data presented in Table 1.

claims.claim: Stone tools used to crack open oysters are more intensively used on Boi Yai Island compared to Lobi Bay.
claims.source: Stone tools used to crack open oysters are more intensively used on Boi Yai Island compared to Lobi Bay (Figure 4, Mann-Whitney U test: U = 32, N1 = 10, N2 = 26, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of use wear data presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Stone tools used to crack Thais bitubercularis shells show more intensive use wear on Boi Yai Island compared to Lobi Bay.
claims.source: Similar results can be found for UWG on stone tools used to crack Thais bitubercularis shells (Figure 4, Mann-Whitney U test: U = 1.5, N1 = 9, N2 = 12, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of use wear data and illustrated in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The three morphologically similar marine snails (Nerita spp., Monodonta Labio and Morulla spp.) produced little inter-group variation in tool use wear intensity.
claims.source: The three morphologically similar marine snails (Nerita spp., Monodonta Labio and Morulla spp.) however, produced little in terms of inter-group UWG variation of tool intensity (Figure 4, Mann-Whitney U test: U = 381.5, N1 = 27, N2 = 29, p=0.832).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference and illustrated in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Macaques in Lobi Bay selected heavier tools than on Boi Yai Island for processing marine snails.
claims.source: For marine snails, we found that macaques in Lobi Bay selected heavier tools than on Boi Yai Island (Figure 5A, Linear model: E = −1.100 SE = 0.176 F(1,54)=38.898 P<0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using a linear model and illustrated in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: When preying on Thais bitubercularis, both populations selected similarly sized tools.
claims.source: When preying on Thais bitubercularis however, both populations selected similarly sized tools (Figure 5B, Linear model: E = −0.099 SE = 0.194 F(1,19)=0.263 P=0.614).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference and illustrated in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The size of the available prey was similar at both Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay sites for C. bifasciatus, marine snails, and Thais bitubercularis.
claims.source: The size of the available prey was similar at both sites (Figure 6, site comparison C. bifasciatus: Mann-Whitney U test: z = −1.368, N1 = 21, N2 = 73, p=0.086; island comparison marine snails: Mann-Whitney U test: z = −0.511, N1 = 123, N2 = 129, p=0.305, island comparison Thais bitubercularis: Mann-Whitney U test: z = −0.458, N1 = 14, N2 = 88, p=0.324).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analyses showing no significant differences in prey size and illustrated in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Macaques on Boi Yai Island used heavier tools than those used for processing oysters in Lobi Bay.
claims.source: To exploit oysters, however, macaques on Boi Yai Island used heavier tools than those used for processing the same prey in Lobi Bay (Figure 7, Linear model: E = 0.451 SE = 0.181 F(1,34)=6.197 P=0.018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using a linear model and illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Oyster size on Boi Yai Island were, in general, larger than in Lobi Bay.
claims.source: Oyster size on Boi Yai Island were, in general, larger than in Lobi Bay (Figure 8, Mann-Whitney U test: z = −2.862, N1 = 341, N2 = 436, p=0.002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of oyster measurements and illustrated in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Several (n = 7) stone tools on Boi Yai Island showed multiple use wear patterns indicative of being used on more than one prey species.
claims.source: Several (n = 7) stone tools on Boi Yai Island showed multiple use wear patterns (on the face and on the tip of the tool). Using the methods of Haslam et al. (2013), these damage patterns are indicative of being used on more than one prey species.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on use wear analysis of stone tools using established methods.

claims.claim: Average weight of available raw material differed between Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay sites when separated between intertidal and tidal zones.
claims.source: Average weight of available raw material (bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals), separated between intertidal and tidal zones differed between sites (Figure 9A, Mann-Whitney U test: z = −5.107, N1 = 270, N2 = 432, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of raw material measurements and illustrated in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: The raw material availability differed between Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay sites.
claims.source: The raw material availability also differed between sites (bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals over observed plots) (Mann-Whitney U test: z = −1.911, N1 = 20, N2 = 24, p=0.028).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of raw material availability data.

claims.claim: Availability of raw material on Boi Yai Island shows a trend towards more stones available in the intertidal zone.
claims.source: However, when separated by tidal and intertidal zones only, availability on Boi Yai Island shows a trend towards more stones available in the intertidal zone (Figure 9B, Mann-Whitney U test: z = −1.374, N1 = 20, N2 = 23, p=0.085).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing a trend (though not statistically significant at p<0.05) and illustrated in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: The availability of raw material in the tidal zone is similar at both Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay sites.
claims.source: The availability in the tidal zone is similar at both sites (Figure 9B, Mann-Whitney U test: z = −1.214, N1 = 20, N2 = 24, p=0.112).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant difference and illustrated in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: Macaques adjust tool size to prey size.
claims.source: The heavier weight of oyster tools used on Boi Yai Island is therefore not surprising and reiterates previous findings, supporting that macaques adjust tool size to prey size (Luncz et al., 2017b; Gumert et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research and is consistent with current findings.

claims.claim: Functional fixedness in regard to stone tool behavioural patterns and target foods can be observed across all tool using non-human primates.
claims.source: Functional fixedness in regard to stone tool behavioural patterns and target foods can be observed across all tool using non-human primates (Carvalho et al., 2008; Fragaszy et al., 2010; Luncz et al., 2016a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on primate tool use.

claims.claim: Variation in available raw material does not explain the differences in stone tool selection between Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay for marine snails.
claims.source: Variation in available raw material does not explain the differences in stone tool selection, as the mean weight of available raw material was in fact greater on Boi Yai Island.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the raw material availability data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Suitable raw material was available in greater quantities along the shore (especially in the intertidal zone) on Boi Yai Island.
claims.source: Furthermore, suitable raw material was available in greater quantities along the shore (especially in the intertidal zone) on Boi Yai Island.
claims.evidence: This is based on the raw material availability data collected in the study.

claims.claim: Purely ecological or environmental factors only account for some of the stone tool variation observed between Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay populations.
claims.source: Based on this evidence, it is possible to suggest that purely ecological or environmental factors only account for some of the stone tool variation observed between these populations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined analysis of ecological, environmental, and tool use data.

claims.claim: The Boi Yai Island tools showed a higher degree of use wear intensity compared to Lobi Bay across oyster and Thais bitubercularis tools.
claims.source: Compared to Lobi Bay, the Boi Yai Island tools showed a higher degree of use wear intensity. This pattern was recorded across oyster and Thais bitubercularis tools.
claims.evidence: This is based on the use wear analysis data presented in the study.

claims.claim: The intensity of use wear seen on oyster tools of Boi Yai Island is unlikely to have developed during a single foraging event.
claims.source: The intensity of use wear seen on oyster tools of Boi Yai Island, however, is unlikely to have developed during a single foraging event (Haslam et al., 2016c).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on use wear analysis and supported by citation to published research on use wear development.

claims.claim: Thais bitubercularis tools used on Boi Yai were characterised by the development of substantial central pits, suggesting multiple re-use events.
claims.source: Thais bitubercularis tools used on Boi Yai were characterised by the development of substantial central pits, suggesting multiple re-use events
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed use wear patterns on the tools.

claims.claim: The hammerstones used to process Thais bitubercularis on Lobi Bay showed few signs of percussive damage.
claims.source: whilst the hammerstones used to process the same species on Lobi Bay showed few signs of percussive damage.
claims.evidence: This is based on the use wear analysis of tools from Lobi Bay.

claims.claim: The relative fragility of marine snail prey species means that little force was required to open them, consequently use wear intensity is low for these tools on both islands.
claims.source: It is reasonable to suggest that the relative fragility of these prey species means that little force was required to open them. Consequently, use wear intensity is low for these tools on both islands.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the prey and the observed use wear patterns.

claims.claim: Lobi Bay appears relatively sheltered compared to Boi Yai Island as it lies within a large bay.
claims.source: Lobi Bay however, appears relatively sheltered compared to Boi Yai Island as it lies within a large bay.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the geographic characteristics of the study sites.

claims.claim: A single example of a granite hammerstone was identified within the Boi Yai assemblage.
claims.source: A single example of a granite hammerstone was identified within the Boi Yai assemblage (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the tool assemblage analysis presented in Table 1.

claims.claim: Granite is more dense than the available limestone rocks which may have been a factor in its selection and re-use as a hammerstone.
claims.source: This igneous rock is more dense than the available limestone rocks available to the macaques which may have been a factor in its selection and re-use as a hammerstone.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the reason for selection based on material properties.

claims.claim: Any available granite has been geologically transported to Boi Yai Island from elsewhere and is therefore very rare.
claims.source: Of course, the re-use of this rock may be coincidental, and it should be remembered that any available granite has been geologically transported to Boi Yai Island from elsewhere and is therefore very rare (Luncz et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This is based on geological knowledge and citation to prior published work.

claims.claim: Raw material availability is consistent between both Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay, with limestone constituting most of the available raw material.
claims.source: As shown previously, raw material availability is consistent between both islands, with limestone constituting most of the available raw material.
claims.evidence: This is based on the raw material survey data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Scarcity of raw material cannot explain the apparent preference for tool re-use on Boi Yai Island.
claims.source: Scarcity of raw material, cannot, therefore, explain the apparent preference for tool re-use on Boi Yai Island.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the raw material availability data.

claims.claim: Raw material availability on Boi Yai Island is greater than that found at Lobi Bay.
claims.source: Indeed, raw material availability on Boi Yai Island is greater than that found at Lobi Bay.
claims.evidence: This is based on the raw material availability data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Macaques on Boi Yai Island preferentially re-use tools rather than choose from readily available and suitable local stones.
claims.source: This would suggest that macaques on Boi Yai Island, unlike their neighbours, preferentially re-use tools rather than choose from readily available and suitable local stones.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined analysis of use wear intensity and raw material availability.

claims.claim: The tool use variation observed between Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay primate populations meets the criteria for tool curation as discussed in the hominin archaeological literature.
claims.source: The tool use variation observed between these two island primate populations meets the criteria for tool curation as discussed in the hominin archaeological literature.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of archaeological theory.

claims.claim: Shott and Sillitoe (2005) define lithic tool curation as the 'ratio of realized to maximum utility' of a tool.
claims.source: Shott and Sillitoe (2005) define lithic tool curation as the 'ratio of realized to maximum utility' of a tool.
claims.evidence: This is a direct citation of a definition from published archaeological literature.

claims.claim: The macaques on Boi Yai Island are successfully extracting a greater degree of utility from their hammerstones compared to those used on Lobi Bay.
claims.source: The varying degrees of repeated use, shown by use wear assessments of the hammerstones between the two islands, coupled with the similarities in primate species, raw material availability, processed prey species, and local ecological settings, suggest that the macaques on Boi Yai Island are successfully extracting a greater degree of utility from their hammerstones compared to those used on Lobi Bay.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined analysis of use wear, ecology, and raw material data.

claims.claim: The variations in the intensity of tool use suggest a primate example of curated stone tool use on Boi Yai Island compared to those on Lobi Bay.
claims.source: These variations in the intensity of tool use suggest a primate example of curated stone tool use on Boi Yai Island compared to those on Lobi Bay.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of archaeological concepts of curation.

claims.claim: Tool differences between wild macaque groups were previously only known to be influenced by prey size.
claims.source: Previously, tool differences between wild macaque groups were only known to be influenced by prey size (Tan et al., 2015; Luncz et al., 2017b; Gumert and Malaivijitnond, 2013)
claims.evidence: This is a statement about prior knowledge supported by citations to published research.

claims.claim: Tool differences between wild macaque groups were previously known to be influenced by sex of the tool user.
claims.source: Previously, tool differences between wild macaque groups were only known to be influenced by prey size (Tan et al., 2015; Luncz et al., 2017b; Gumert and Malaivijitnond, 2013) or sex of the tool user (Gumert et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about prior knowledge supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: The frequency of tool use in long-tailed macaques might be influenced by genetics, where the Burmese subspecies (Macaca fascicularis aurea) and hybrids expressing a more Burmese phenotype use tools in higher frequencies.
claims.source: Furthermore, it has been shown that the frequency of tool use in long-tailed macaques might be influenced by genetics, where the Burmese subspecies (Macaca fascicularis aurea) and hybrids expressing a more Burmese phenotype use tools in higher frequencies (Gumert et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published research on genetic influences on tool use.

claims.claim: The research sites in the Ao Phang Nga National Park lie within a natural hybrid zone.
claims.source: Our research sites in the Ao Phang Nga National Park lie within a natural hybrid zone and phylogenetic differences between groups cannot yet be fully excluded.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the geographic and genetic context of the study populations.

claims.claim: Preliminary data show similar degrees of hybridization between groups at Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay.
claims.source: Preliminary data show similar degrees of hybridization between groups (Malaivijitnond et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published genetic data.

claims.claim: The demographics do not differ between the two populations at Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay.
claims.source: The demographics (assessed from video footage, Luncz et al., 2017a) do not differ between the two populations.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on demographic assessment from video footage cited in prior work.

claims.claim: Males and females of all age classes use stone tools in both populations.
claims.source: Males and females of all age classes use stone tools, it therefore seems unlikely that the difference in stone tools between the two islands stem from these factors.
claims.evidence: This is based on observational data about tool use demographics.

claims.claim: Macaques of Lobi Bay and Boi Yai Island do not forage on Cerith bifasciatus, despite its widespread abundance.
claims.source: Additionally, by combining our new results here with our previous findings of tool use by macaques in the Gulf of Thailand (Luncz et al., 2017b), we were able to identify that macaques of Lobi Bay and Boi Yai Island do not forage on Cerith bifasciatus, despite its widespread abundance.
claims.evidence: This is based on the absence of evidence for this prey species in the tool assemblages combined with prey availability data.

claims.claim: Macaques in the Gulf of Thailand regularly exploit Cerith bifasciatus.
claims.source: Macaques in the Gulf of Thailand, however, regularly exploit this species.
claims.evidence: This is based on prior published research on macaque foraging behavior.

claims.claim: Tool selection can be explained by ecological, biological and environmental factors.
claims.source: These results partly support previous research that has shown that tool selection can be explained by ecological, biological and environmental factors (Gumert et al., 2011; Gumert and Malaivijitnond, 2013; Luncz et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published research and is partially supported by current findings.

claims.claim: The differences in use wear intensity and frequency of re-use of hammerstones on Boi Yai Island remains unexplained by ecological, biological and environmental factors.
claims.source: However, the differences in use wear intensity and therefore frequency of re-use of hammerstones on Boi Yai Island remains unexplained by these factors.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis showing that known factors do not fully explain the observed variation.

claims.claim: Tool use across a synchronous landscape need not be uniform.
claims.source: Our new results show differences in use wear intensity and the extent to which macaques unintentionally modify the shape of their tools through use. This would suggest that tool use across a synchronous landscape need not be uniform
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed differences in tool use between the two populations.

claims.claim: Tool variation may be conditioned by cultural factors as well as responses to ecological conditions.
claims.source: Indeed, tool variation may be conditioned by cultural factors as well as responses to ecological conditions.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for the observed variation.

claims.claim: Tool use has been shown to be influenced by social learning in several species.
claims.source: Tool use has been shown to be influenced by social learning in several species (van Schaik et al., 1999; Whiten, 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on social learning in primates.

claims.claim: Distinct cultural differences in technological behaviour in living primates has mainly been associated with the ape clade.
claims.source: To date, distinct cultural differences in technological behaviour in living primates has mainly been associated with the ape clade (Whiten et al., 1999; Whiten and Boesch, 2001; van Shaik, 2004; Luncz et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on primate culture.

claims.claim: When raw material availability, species differences, functional differences and environmental and ecological conditions are shared and do not explain stone tool variation, the effect of cultural differences as a driving factor behind lithic technological variation in hominins must not be overlooked.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that when raw material availability, species differences, functional differences and environmental and ecological conditions are shared and do not explain stone tool variation the effect of cultural differences as a driving factor behind lithic technological variation in hominins must not be overlooked (Koops et al., 2015; Luncz et al., 2015; Pascual-Garrido, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about implications for hominin archaeology based on the primate data and supported by citations to related research.

claims.claim: Tool selection in old world monkeys might be affected through social learning and therefore might classify as a cultural behaviour.
claims.source: Our results highlight the possibility that tool selection in old world monkeys might also be affected through social learning and therefore might classify as a cultural behaviour.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings for understanding cultural behavior in monkeys.

claims.claim: Increased human contact is known to affect stone tool behaviour by altering natural foraging behaviours in long-tailed macaques.
claims.source: Increased human contact is known to affect stone tool behaviour by altering natural foraging behaviours (Gumert et al., 2013; Luncz et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on human impacts on macaque behavior.

claims.claim: Long-tailed macaques are experiencing profound population threats.
claims.source: Long-tailed macaques are experiencing profound population threats (Eudey, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published conservation literature.

claims.claim: Data was collected in January and February 2017 and 2018 on two shorelines at islands in the Ao Phang Nga National Park.
claims.source: We collected data in January and February 2017 and 2018 on two shorelines at islands in the Ao Phang Nga National Park.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing and location of data collection.

claims.claim: Lobi Bay is located in the northwest tip of Yao Noi Island (8°10′ 51.06' N, 98° 37′ 42.52' E).

results.result: Macaques on Boi Yai Island show significantly higher use wear intensity on tools used for oysters and Thais bitubercularis compared to Lobi Bay, indicating more intensive tool reuse. For marine snails, use wear intensity was similar between sites. The higher use wear on Boi Yai tools suggests multiple reuse events, particularly for oyster and Thais bitubercularis processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34, C50-C54 provide converging statistical evidence (Mann-Whitney U tests with p<0.001) and use wear analysis showing differential tool reuse patterns between sites. The statistical tests are appropriate, sample sizes are adequate (N=115 tools total), and the use wear grading system (Table 2) provides a validated methodology. Figures 2-4 provide visual confirmation of the patterns.

results.result: For marine snails of similar size at both sites, macaques in Lobi Bay selected significantly heavier tools than those on Boi Yai Island, despite greater raw material availability on Boi Yai. This pattern cannot be explained by ecological or environmental factors alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 provide statistical support (linear models and Mann-Whitney U tests with appropriate p-values) showing tool selection differences despite similar prey sizes. Claims C47-C49 demonstrate that raw material availability does not explain this pattern, as Boi Yai actually has greater availability. The inference that ecological factors alone cannot explain the variation is logically sound given the data.

results.result: Macaques on Boi Yai Island used heavier tools to process larger oysters compared to Lobi Bay, consistent with the principle that macaques adjust tool size to prey size.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 provide statistical evidence (linear model p=0.018, Mann-Whitney U test p=0.002) showing both tool weight and oyster size differences between sites. Claim C45 contextualizes this within prior research. This result is well-supported and replicates previous findings, though it represents an expected ecological adaptation rather than a novel discovery.

results.result: Raw material availability was greater on Boi Yai Island than Lobi Bay, particularly in the intertidal zone, yet macaques on Boi Yai preferentially reused tools rather than selecting from abundant available stones. This pattern suggests tool curation behavior independent of raw material scarcity.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 provide statistical evidence from systematic transect surveys with appropriate bootstrapping methods. Claims C59-C62 draw logical inferences from this data combined with use wear patterns. The conclusion that raw material scarcity cannot explain tool reuse on Boi Yai is well-supported, as availability is actually greater there. However, the study acknowledges (C55) that tidal forces could affect tool availability, which represents a potential confound requiring future research.

results.result: The tool use variation between Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay meets archaeological criteria for tool curation, with Boi Yai macaques extracting greater utility from their hammerstones through repeated use compared to Lobi Bay.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 apply established archaeological definitions (C64, citing Shott and Sillitoe 2005) to the primate data. The inference is logically sound given the demonstrated differences in use wear intensity (C32-C33, C50) combined with similar ecological settings and raw material availability. The application of archaeological concepts to primate behavior is appropriate and well-justified.

results.result: Tool selection and reuse patterns in long-tailed macaques cannot be entirely explained by ecological diversity, suggesting that tool use may develop differently within species and that cultural factors may influence material culture variation at local geographic scales.
results.evaluation: While claims C3, C49, and C77 correctly identify that ecological factors do not fully explain the observed variation, the leap to cultural explanations (C79, C82, C83) is speculative. The study acknowledges multiple uncontrolled factors: genetic differences cannot be fully excluded (C70), demographic data is limited (C72), and the study relies on archaeological inference rather than direct behavioral observation. Alternative explanations such as individual learning histories, group-specific foraging traditions, or unmeasured environmental factors have not been systematically ruled out. The cultural interpretation is plausible but requires additional evidence.

results.result: Genetic and demographic factors are unlikely to explain the observed tool use differences between Boi Yai and Lobi Bay populations, as both populations show similar hybridization levels and mixed demographics with tool use across all age and sex classes.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 provide some evidence for similarity between populations, but the evidence is limited. Claim C71 cites only preliminary data from 2007, and C72 relies on video footage assessment rather than systematic demographic surveys. Claim C70 explicitly acknowledges that phylogenetic differences cannot be fully excluded. The genetic analysis cited (C92) is unpublished ('in prep'), limiting independent verification. While the authors argue these factors are unlikely explanations, the evidence is insufficient to definitively rule them out.

results.result: Macaques at Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay do not forage on Cerith bifasciatus despite its widespread abundance, while macaques in the Gulf of Thailand regularly exploit this species, suggesting population-specific prey preferences.
results.evaluation: Claim C74 is based on the absence of C. bifasciatus in tool assemblages combined with prey availability surveys showing its abundance. Claim C75 provides comparative context from prior research. The inference of population-specific prey preferences is reasonable, though the mechanism (cultural transmission vs. ecological differences between regions) remains unclear. The evidence supports the observation but not necessarily the cultural interpretation.

results.result: A single granite hammerstone was identified on Boi Yai Island, which may have been preferentially selected and reused due to its greater density compared to available limestone, though this could be coincidental given granite's rarity.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 documents the observation (n=1), but claims C57-C58 acknowledge the interpretation is speculative. A single example is insufficient to establish a pattern of preferential selection. The authors appropriately note this may be coincidental, and the rarity of granite (C58) makes it difficult to assess whether this represents intentional selection or chance. This observation is interesting but requires more data to draw firm conclusions.

results.result: The study sites at Boi Yai Island and Lobi Bay are well-characterized in terms of location, geology, macaque populations, and prey species, with appropriate methodological criteria for identifying used tools.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C99 provide comprehensive methodological and site characterization information. Geographic coordinates are provided (C87-C88), geological context is established with citations (C94-C97), and tool identification criteria are clearly defined (C98-C99). The 20 cm distance criterion (C99) is reasonable though somewhat arbitrary. Population characteristics are documented through prior research (C91-C92), though genetic data remains unpublished. Overall, the site characterization and methods are adequately described.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on stone tool use in hominins and non-human primates, establishing the context for primate archaeology and prior findings on macaque tool use variation related to ecological factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C29 provide well-cited background information establishing the field of primate archaeology and prior research findings. These claims are appropriately supported by citations to published literature and represent accurate summaries of prior work. This contextual information is essential for framing the current study but does not constitute new findings.

results.result: Tool selection in primates is influenced by ecological factors and shows functional fixedness, with social learning documented in several species, though cultural differences in technological behavior have primarily been associated with apes rather than monkeys.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46, C76, C80-C81 accurately summarize established findings from prior research with appropriate citations. These claims provide important context for interpreting the current findings but represent synthesis of existing knowledge rather than new discoveries. The citations support the statements made.

results.result: Long-tailed macaques face population threats and their tool use behavior can be affected by increased human contact, highlighting conservation concerns for these populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 are supported by appropriate citations to published conservation and behavioral research. These claims provide important context for the conservation implications of the research but are not primary findings of the current study.
